newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Forex loans raise concern at Bank of Israel.
newsitem.headline: Forex loans raise concern at Bank of Israel.

text.p: Bank of Israel Supervisor of Banks Zeev Abeles on Sunday expressed concern about the growing trend of taking out loans linked to foreign currency.
He said it exposes those taking such loans to risks in devaluations.

"I think the banks have to check very thoroughly the ability to repay loans and the sources of repayment of customers who ask for foreign currency credit and to make more stringent the requirements and collateral required for this type of credit," Abeles said at a news conference.

"I expect the banks to act with caution and responsibility because the realisation of this risk could call in to question the ability of these customers to repay their debts and consequently roll over the risk and the losses to the banks."
The supervisor of banks department is following the situation closely and examining its implications for the stability of the banks.
"If we see that the banks are exposing themselves to too much risk in this area we intend to intervene," he said, adding that the banks were being looked at individually.

High domestic interest rates in the past two years have increased the attractiveness of such loans. Foreign currency linked credit grew from $6.5 billion at the end of 1994 to $14.7 billion at end of 1996 and to $16.8 billion at the end of the first quarter of 1997.
The share of foreign currency linked credit in total bank credit increased from 14 percent in 1994 to 24.2 percent in 1996 and 29 percent at the end of the first quarter of 1997.
The main recipients were the construction, food and financial services industries.
Abeles also expressed concern about the rise in the banks' operating costs, mainly labour-related costs due to special programmes to encourage early retirement.
From 1990 to 1996 operational costs grew 25 percent or 3.8 percent a year while labour costs alone grew 4.3 percent a year or 29 percent.

Abeles also cautioned that many factors that contributed to the banks' profits in 1996 and the first quarter of 1997 were short-term factors. High interest rates, for example, led companies to take foreign currency loans and investors to switch from provident funds to savings accounts.
A weak capital market forced companies to seek out bank financing since they could not raise money on the bourse.
An economic slowdown will take its toll on the banks later in the year, he said.
Abeles said there has been a decline in interest from foreign banks in opening branches in Israel because of the geopolitical situation but he would not elaborate.
